1	# PR Description Writing
2	
3	How to resolve the right commit range and compose a PR title and body. Loaded on demand by `spec-commit-push-pr` callers — do not load earlier.
4	
5	Step Pre-A resolves the commit range, diff, and (for existing PRs) the current PR body. Steps A through H assume Pre-A's outputs are in context.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Core principle
10	
11	The diff is already visible on GitHub. The description exists to explain what the diff cannot show: what was impossible before and is now possible, what was broken and is now fixed, and which shape changed. Cut any sentence a reader could reconstruct from the diff itself.
12	
13	- Bad (lists what was edited): "Adds `branch-creation.md`, modifies `spec-commit-push-pr/SKILL.md`, and updates contract tests."
14	- Good: "Default-branch shipping now verifies a fresh base before any PR work touches the branch."
15	- Bad (states how the work was done): "The shipping reference now anchors branch verification to a named checklist."
16	- Good: "Shipping to the default branch now catches a stale base before any PR work touches the branch."
17	
18	If the lead sentence describes what was edited rather than what is now different for someone using this, rewrite it — this applies to every section, not just the opening, and restating the diff is the default failure mode this reference exists to prevent. A mechanism written in an outcome's grammar is judged by the same condition: "now anchors its checks to a named framework" is how the work was done, while a mechanism that *is* what the reader gets stays.
19	
20	For user-facing bugs, run an extra before/after pass before writing the mechanism: name what the user would have seen before and what they now see instead. Only then mention the technical cause or fix, and only if it helps the reviewer understand risk.
21	
22	---
23	
24	## Project PR-body contract
25	
26	Before composition, use active project instructions, then inspect standard PR-template locations relative to the confirmed repository root: root `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, `docs/`, `.github/` and `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/`. Read only applicable templates and directly referenced contribution guidance. Resolve multiple templates from the caller's change category or existing PR; ask only if a consequential template choice remains unresolved.
27	
28	Required headings, fields, order, checklists and boilerplate outrank this reference's default layout. A minimum template permits useful additions; an exact/template-only contract does not. Preserve truthful unchecked/not-run fields rather than checking them by inference. Fit outcomes, validation and provenance into permitted sections; suppress optional teaching, diagrams and footer when the contract forbids them. Do not scan unrelated documentation or create a template parser.
29	
30	## Step Pre-A: Resolve the PR commit range and diff
31	
32	Determine which commits and diff the description should cover. Run this first; Steps A and beyond assume the commit list and full diff are in context.
33	
34	### Mode
35	
36	- **Current-branch mode.** Describe the captured HEAD vs the caller's resolved base, otherwise the confirmed default base. Used when the caller has no explicit PR reference (Step 6 of spec-commit-push-pr's full workflow; description-only mode without a PR ref).
37	- **PR mode.** Describe a specific PR's commit range. Used by the Description Update workflow (the existing PR on the current branch) and description-only mode (the user pasted a PR URL/number). The PR ref may be a bare number, `#NN`, `pr:NN`, or a full URL — the caller passes it to `gh pr view <ref>` directly. (`gh pr view` accepts numbers and URLs natively; `#NN` and `pr:NN` need the `#` or `pr:` stripped before passing.)
38	
39	### Resolve PR metadata (PR mode and current-branch-with-existing-PR)
40	
41	```text
42	gh pr view <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo> --json number,baseRefName,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefOid,headRepository,headRepositoryOwner,isCrossRepository,url,body,state
43	```
44	
45	If the returned `state` is not `OPEN`, report `"PR <number> is <state>; cannot generate description"` and exit gracefully — do not invent a description.
46	
47	### Detect the base branch and remote
48	
49	For PR mode (or current-branch mode with an existing PR), use `baseRefName` from the metadata above. For current-branch mode without an existing PR, resolve in priority order:
50	
51	1. **Caller-supplied base** (if the caller passed `base:<ref>`) — validate it in the confirmed base repository; do not substitute a same-named ref from a fork.
52	2. **Repo default branch** — `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref origin/HEAD`, strip `origin/` prefix.
53	3. **GitHub metadata** — `gh repo view <host/owner/repo> --json defaultBranchRef`. Parse the returned value; do not guess from common branch names.
54	
55	If none resolve, keep the base unresolved and ask only for that missing fact. A local branch named main is not evidence of the intended base.
56	
57	For the **base remote**, parse `owner/repo` from the PR URL (or use the repo of the current checkout in current-branch mode without a PR) and match against `git remote -v` fetch URLs (handle both `git@github.com:owner/repo` and `https://github.com/owner/repo` forms; strip `.git`). The matching remote name is `<base-remote>`. **If no remote matches** (fork-based PR with no `upstream` remote), do NOT default to `origin` — `origin` would diff against the wrong base. Skip directly to Case B.
58	
59	### Case A — base remote matched, attempt local git
60	
61	Bind the description to exact source identity. In PR mode use the metadata's `baseRefOid` and `headRefOid`, never a potentially stale `<remote>/<branch>` merely because it resolves. In current-branch mode capture HEAD and the resolved base commit; disclose a cached/offline base as such. Full shipping uses the separate fresh-base contract in `branch-creation.md`.
62	
63	Run each command separately, replacing placeholders with validated literal values and inspecting the actual exit status:
64	
65	```text
66	git rev-parse --verify <base-sha>^{commit}
67	git rev-parse --verify <head-sha>^{commit}
68	git merge-base <base-sha> <head-sha>
69	git log --oneline <merge-base>..<head-sha>
70	git diff <merge-base>...<head-sha>
71	```
72	
73	Fetch only missing objects from the matched base remote. Capture and validate each result before consuming it; do not use shell variables, pipelines, redirects or command substitution to hide failures. If merge-base fails, use the API fallback for a known PR rather than inventing a range. Uncommitted changes are context only and must not be described as published PR contents.
74	
75	### Case A inner fallback — SHA fetch rejected
76	
77	When a PR head SHA fetch is rejected, a separate single-ref fetch may retrieve `refs/pull/<number>/head` from the confirmed base repository:
78	
79	```text
80	git fetch --no-tags <base-remote> refs/pull/<number>/head
81	git rev-parse --verify FETCH_HEAD
82	```
83	
84	Capture the returned SHA immediately and compare it with the metadata head. A mismatch requires refreshed PR metadata and a newly bound range; do not quietly compose against mixed revisions. Missing base objects still require a valid fetch or API fallback. Never parse FETCH_HEAD with shell-specific awk/substitution or assume the last of multiple fetched refs is the PR head.
85	
86	### Case B — API only
87	
88	Use Case B when:
89	- No local remote matches the PR's base repo (fork-PR, cross-repo PR), OR
90	- Case A's fetches all fail (offline, restricted network, expired auth, GHES quirks blocking both SHA and `refs/pull/N/head`).
91	
92	Skip local git entirely:
93	
94	```text
95	gh pr diff <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo>
96	gh pr view <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo> --json commits,headRefOid,baseRefOid
97	```
98	
99	Read metadata again after API diff/commit retrieval and compare both head/base SHAs. If either changed, discard the mixed snapshot and refresh within a bounded retry; continued movement leaves composition pending. Note the API fallback and source identity in the caller handoff. Without a known PR and a valid local range, return the missing evidence instead of guessing.
100	
101	### Empty range
102	
103	If the resulting commit list is empty (HEAD already merged into the base, or the branch has no unique commits), report `"No commits to describe"` and exit gracefully — do not invent a description.
104	
105	---
106	
107	## Step A: Classify commits
108	
109	Scan the commit list and classify each commit:
110	
111	- **Feature commits** -- implement the PR's purpose (new functionality, intentional refactors, design changes). These drive the description.
112	- **Fix-up commits** -- iteration work (code review fixes, lint fixes, test fixes, rebase resolutions, style cleanups). Invisible to the reader.
113	
114	When sizing the description, mentally subtract fix-up commits: a branch with 12 commits but 9 fix-ups is a 3-commit PR.
115	
116	Build a compact **scope map** from the complete oneline commit list and final three-dot diff resolved in Pre-A. Use subjects for full-range coverage, then use the final diff to merge overlapping work, remove fix-up-only outcomes, and correct stale subjects. Read fuller messages only when a subject remains unclear or contradicts the diff. Group material outcomes into clusters, identify each cluster's claims, and name one umbrella outcome covering them. Never derive that umbrella from the latest commit, tracker title, branch name, original request, or opening incident alone. The story of how work started is one cluster's origin, not the whole change.
117	
118	Check program placement using only context already available: the user request, a known plan, existing PR body, commit messages, or explicit series language. If this is part of a program, name the program outcome, this PR's contribution, and known preceding or follow-on work. Do not invent a series or scan all open PRs just for this check.
119	
120	Before composing, write the finished map as a short run-local working note: umbrella outcome; clusters and their material claims; program placement or `none`. State the umbrella as what is now different for someone using this, never as the mechanism that produced it — the title and the opening both inherit the map's altitude, so a mechanism-shaped umbrella is not something a later step can correct. Keep it to three or four lines. This is drafting context, not another section to publish in the PR body. Step H audits the title and opening against this written map rather than memory.
121	
122	---
123	
124	## Step B: Decide on evidence
125	
126	Decide whether to include an evidence section in the body.
127	
128	**Evidence is useful** when the diff changes behavior or makes a material claim a reviewer cannot establish from the diff alone: UI, CLI output, API behavior with runnable code, generated artifacts, workflow output, ranking or scoring logic, deployment/config behavior, migrations, performance, or compatibility.
129	
130	**Evidence is normally unnecessary** for:
131	- Inert documentation, changelog-only edits, release metadata, test-only changes, or pure internal refactors with no material reviewer claim
132	- Behavior requiring unavailable credentials, paid/cloud services, bot tokens, deploy-only infrastructure, or hardware not provided
133	
134	Classify files by runtime purpose, not extension. Markdown or YAML may be inert prose, but it may also be runtime agent instructions, configuration, generated product content, policy code, or deployment behavior. Do not auto-skip evidence merely because a change is labeled docs-only or uses a prose-oriented extension.
135	
136	**Decision logic:**
137	
138	1. **Existing PR body contains a `## Demo` or `## Screenshots` section with image embeds:** preserve it verbatim unless the user's focus asks to refresh or remove it. Include the preserved block in the body.
139	2. **No existing evidence block:** omit the evidence section entirely unless the caller already captured evidence and passed it in.
140	
141	Do not label test output as "Demo" or "Screenshots". Place any preserved evidence block before the Spec-First footer.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Step B1: Related work and closing semantics
146	
147	Collect known references from the request, caller handoff, current PR body, selected template and already-available commit/plan/debug context. Read a relevant fuller commit message only when its reference or intent is unclear. Do not search for plans or scan unrelated issues to manufacture provenance.
148	
149	Distinguish a closing reference from a neutral relationship. Closing requires evidence that the PR fully resolves the item, known tracker syntax and the actual target conditions. For GitHub Issues, use closing keywords only when targeting the confirmed default branch and resolving the whole issue; a partial fix, investigation, validation-only change or non-default target gets a neutral link. Preserve exact cross-repository identity with a full URL or `owner/repo#number`. Unknown tracker semantics or uncertain intent never acquire closing keywords.
150	
151	On rewrite, preserve existing related references and their meaning. If an existing closing line conflicts with the verified scope/target, retain the reference as neutral and explain that correction; do not silently keep a harmful close or drop its provenance. Follow project tracker conventions without imposing a universal label. Keep non-closing IDs in a separate neutral related-work line, away from close/fix/resolve phrases that integrations could interpret as actions. A PR body can trigger tracker automation; writing style does not authorize an additional tracker action.
152	
153	---
154	
155	## Step B2: Judge new concepts
156	
157	Decide whether the change introduces a concept: a pattern, technique, library, or domain idea that a reader of this repo would plausibly not know. Skip this step entirely when the skill's concept teaching gate is off or the project's exact-template contract forbids the section.
158	
159	**Gather candidates from the diff first.** Read the Pre-A diff for concept-shaped novelty: a dependency put to first real use, a technique the diff visibly introduces, or a domain idea the code now encodes. Most PRs surface no candidate; stop there and compose no section. Absence is the common case, and this path costs zero extra tool calls.
160	
161	**Check each candidate against the base ref, never the working tree.** The working tree contains this PR's own code, so grepping it finds the concept you just added and wrongly concludes it is already established. Check the base instead, using the base resolved in Pre-A:
162	
163	```text
164	git grep -il -e <term> <base-sha>
165	```
166	
167	Run one call per candidate. Candidates cap at two, so the cost stays bounded. Inspect the exit status: 0 means matches, 1 means no matches for that term, and other failures leave coverage unknown. Read at most the needed matches; no match alone does not prove a concept is absent under other terminology.
168	
169	A candidate is teachable only when it is both new to this codebase in this PR and transferable beyond it. Never teach routine use of an already-established repo pattern, ordinary refactors, renames, dependency bumps, or project-internal plumbing with no transferable idea. When in doubt, omit; a missing section costs little, while a patronizing one trains readers to skip the feature.
170	
171	In the `gh` fallback path (fork PR, no local base refs), judge from diff context alone and lean conservative: compose the section only when the concept is unmistakably new.
172	
173	- Bad: teaching "dependency injection" because a PR added one constructor argument in a codebase full of DI.
174	- Good: teaching infinite scroll on the PR that replaces pagination with it for the first time.
175	
176	**Compose the section** under the heading `## New concepts` for at most 2 concepts. When more qualify, teach the most load-bearing concepts and name the rest in one sentence. Per concept, write roughly 10-25 lines covering:
177	
178	1. **What it is**: the concept in plain words, no jargon dependency.
179	2. **Why here**: why it was chosen over the obvious alternative this PR could have used.
180	3. **One example from this PR**: how the shipped behavior exercises the concept.
181	4. **When not to use it**: one sentence on the boundary.
182	
183	Format by material:
184	
185	| Material | Show |
186	|----------|------|
187	| Architecture, relationships, boundaries | Fenced `mermaid` block (`flowchart TB`) |
188	| Code behavior, a diff's mechanics | Fenced code block with a one-line why comment above |
189	| A comparison or trade-off | Pipe-delimited table, prose verdict underneath |
190	
191	Lead with the point, then the mechanism, then the caveat. Dense is good; long is not. Never hand-draw box-drawing or ASCII diagrams. The section is additive to Step D's sizing: a small PR that introduces a heavy concept still gets the section, and the section never counts against the base description's size rows.
192	
193	**Rewrite preservation:** when rewriting an existing PR body, preserve an existing `## New concepts` section and any explainer-doc link verbatim, same as `## Demo`, unless the user's focus asks to refresh the concepts. Also preserve caller-written decision-record sections — `## Known Residuals` and `## Post-Deploy Monitoring & Validation` — verbatim: they are durable review records owned by the calling workflow (e.g., `spec-work` shipping), not description prose to regenerate; if they look stale, flag the mismatch in the handoff instead of silently dropping them. Description-only and description-update runs never write repo files.
194	
195	**Archival hook:** when `spec-commit-push-pr` confirms the apply and `pr_teaching_archive` is on in full workflow, the teaching content is also written to `docs/explainers/` and linked from the section. The commit-and-push transition and doc frontmatter live in `references/apply-and-handoff.md` (reached via `SKILL.md` Step 7).
196	
197	---
198	
199	## Step C: Frame the narrative
200	
201	Articulate the PR's narrative frame:
202	
203	Use Step A's written umbrella and material clusters as the frame. Represent peer outcomes at parity instead of making the initiating incident the main story and treating equally material results as extras. When program context exists, decide what the opening's one idea must include: usually the local outcome by itself, with concise placement in a short block after the opening; but when the program is what gives the local outcome its shape or its point, the connection to the program is part of the one idea and belongs in the opening — either half may lead, whichever reads better for this change, and naming which part of the program this PR delivers keeps that opening honest. Never crowd the opening with already-visible mechanisms or a second description of the same outcome; everything the one idea does not need goes in the block after it.
204	
205	1. **Before**: What was broken, limited, or impossible? (One sentence.)
206	2. **After**: What's now possible or improved? (One sentence.)
207	3. **Scope rationale** (only if 2+ separable-looking concerns): Why do these ship together? (One sentence.)
208	
209	This frame becomes the opening. For small+simple PRs, the "after" sentence alone may be the entire description.
210	
211	### Known decision provenance
212	
213	Use only caller-supplied or already-read plan decisions relevant to this diff. Preserve `user-directed`, `user-approved`, delegated agent judgment and inferred assumptions as distinct provenance; `session-settled:` text is a source annotation, not proof of new approval. Mention the selected decision and source only when it helps review. Carry an actual proceed-under-conflict limitation when supplied; do not invent a rejected alternative or reopen settled choices as a backlog. No plan in hand means no plan hunt.
214	
215	### 保留贡献者来源
216	
217	只有本 PR 实际交付了作者之外的人的工作，才补充 contributor credit。已有 PR 以其实际 author 为准；新 PR 以 shipping 人的 Git 身份为线索，并核实其他邮箱别名，不能仅因 email 不同就认定为另一人。证据来自 Pre-A 完整范围内的 commit author、已有 `Co-authored-by` trailer，或本工作继续/替代的明确 PR。模型、harness 或 bot 署名不算人的贡献；独立改写与直接移植的区别沿用 `commit-and-push.md`。
218	
219	适用时在正文署名，并链接已知的前序/被替代 PR；重写保留已有 contributor credit。若仓库文档或当前 repo metadata 确认会 squash merge，将其他实际贡献者的 `Co-authored-by: Name <email>` 放在 body 最后一个段落、全部模板章节和 footer 之后，便于进入 squash message；仅 `squashMergeAllowed` 表示允许该方式，不能当作本 PR 必然 squash 的证据。姓名和邮箱精确复制自 commit author 或已有 trailer；被替代 PR 的提交不在当前 range 时，回源其 commits。邮箱缺失或来源不可核实时只作有证据的正文署名，报告缺口，不拼接邮箱、不制造身份或重写历史。
220	
221	---
222	
223	## Step D: Size by reviewer decision cost
224	
225	Size the description by how much a reviewer cannot establish from the diff alone, not by changed-line count, file extension, or visual surface. A small ranking-logic or deployment edit may carry more uncertainty than a large mechanical rename.
226	
227	Before sizing, name the change's **material claims**: what became possible, what was fixed, what risk changed, and which design decision the reviewer must assess. Note which claims the diff alone cannot establish. Surface those claims and the evidence or residual uncertainty that changes confidence; leave reconstructable mechanics implicit.
228	
229	Decision cost sets what to surface, not permission to write more. Reviewer uncertainty may move a change at most one row in the table below. A small high-uncertainty diff earns a sharper lead and a concise validation caveat, not a multi-section essay. Prefer the shortest description that still lets a reviewer decide.
230	
231	Evidence can include benchmarks, API captures, migration or rollback exercises, logs, compatibility matrices, security analysis, evals, manual probes, and rollout results. Include a result only when it changes confidence in a material claim. Keep demonstrated results distinct from assumptions and mixed or negative outcomes.
232	
233	Subtract fix-up commits when sizing. Large PRs need more selectivity, not more content.
234	
235	| Change profile | Description approach |
236	|---|---|
237	| Small + simple (typo, config, dep bump) | 1-2 sentences, no headers. Under ~300 characters. |
238	| Small + non-trivial (bugfix, behavioral change) | Short narrative, ~3-5 sentences. No headers unless two distinct concerns. |
239	| Medium feature or refactor | Narrative frame (before/after/scope), then what changed and why. Call out design decisions. |
240	| Large or architecturally significant | Narrative frame + up to 3-5 design-decision callouts + 1-2 sentence test summary + key docs links. Target ~100 lines, cap ~150. For PRs with many mechanisms, use a Summary-level table to list them; do NOT create an H3 subsection per mechanism. Reviewers scrutinize decisions, not inventories — the diff and spec files carry the detail. If you find yourself writing 10+ subsections, consolidate to a table. |
241	| Performance improvement | Include before/after measurements if available. Markdown table works well. |
242	
243	The table is calibration, not a diff-size formula. When in doubt, choose the shortest row that still carries the decision-relevant context, evidence, and residual uncertainty.
244	
245	---
246	
247	## Step E: Apply writing principles
248	
249	### Writing voice
250	
251	If the repo has documented style preferences in context, follow those. Otherwise:
252	
253	- Preserve exact identifiers, thresholds, paths, error text and negative results when they carry the claim; plain language must not erase technical meaning.
254	- Active voice. No em dashes or `--` substitutes; use periods, commas, colons, or parentheses.
255	- Vary sentence length. Never three similar-length sentences in a row.
256	- Do not make a claim and immediately explain it. Trust the reader.
257	- Plain English. Technical jargon fine; business jargon never.
258	- No filler: "it's worth noting", "importantly", "essentially", "in order to", "leverage", "utilize."
259	- Digits for numbers ("3 files"), not words ("three files").
260	
261	### Writing principles
262	
263	- **Lead with value**: Open with what's now possible or fixed, not what was moved around. The subtler failure is leading with the mechanism ("Replace the hardcoded capture block with a tiered skill") instead of the outcome ("Evidence capture now works for CLI tools and libraries, not just web apps"). For user-facing bugs, lead with the visible before/after before naming the implementation mechanism.
264	- **No orphaned opening paragraphs**: If the description uses `##` headings anywhere, the opening must also be under a heading (e.g., `## Summary`). For short descriptions with no sections, a bare paragraph is fine.
265	- **Describe the net result, not the journey**: The description covers the end state, not how you got there. No iteration history, debugging steps, intermediate failures, or bugs found and fixed during development. This applies equally when regenerating for an existing PR: rewrite from the current state, not as a log of what changed since the last version. Exception: process details critical to understand a design choice.
266	- **When commits conflict, trust the final diff**: The commit list is supporting context, not the source of truth. If commits describe intermediate steps later revised or reverted, describe the end state from the full branch diff.
267	- **Explain the non-obvious**: If the diff is self-explanatory, don't narrate it. Spend space on things the diff doesn't show: why this approach, what was rejected, what the reviewer should watch.
268	- **Use structure when it earns its keep**: Headers, bullets, and tables aid comprehension, not mandatory template sections.
269	- **Markdown tables for data**: Before/after comparisons, performance numbers, or option trade-offs communicate well as tables.
270	- **No empty sections**: If a section doesn't apply, omit it. No "N/A" or "None."
271	- **Test plan — only when non-obvious**: Include when testing requires edge cases the reviewer wouldn't think of, hard-to-verify behavior, or specific setup. Omit when "run the tests" is the only useful guidance. When the branch adds test files, name them with what they cover.
272	- **No Commits section**: GitHub already shows the commit list in its own tab. A Commits section in the PR body duplicates that without adding context. Omit unless the commits need annotations explaining their ordering or shipping rationale.
273	- **No Review / process section**: Do not include a section describing how the reviewer should review (checklists of things to look at, process bullets). Process doesn't help the reviewer evaluate code. Call out specific non-obvious things to scrutinize inline with the change that warrants it.
274	
275	### Visual communication
276	
277	Include a visual aid only when the change is structurally complex enough that a reviewer would struggle to reconstruct the mental model from prose alone.
278	
279	**The core distinction — structure vs. parallel variation:**
280	
281	- Use a **Mermaid diagram** when the change has **topology** — components with directed relationships (calls, flows, dependencies, state transitions, data paths). Diagrams express "A talks to B, B talks to C, C does not talk back to A" in a way tables cannot.
282	- Use a **markdown table** when the change has **parallel variation of a single shape** — N things that share the same attributes but differ in their values. Tables express "option 1 costs X, option 2 costs Y, option 3 costs Z" cleanly.
283	
284	Architecture changes are almost always topology (components + edges), so Mermaid is usually the right call — a table of "components that interact" loses the edges and becomes a flat list. Reserve tables for genuinely parallel data: before/after measurements, option trade-offs, flag matrices, config enumerations.
285	
286	**When to include (prefer Mermaid, not a table, for architecture/flow):**
287	
288	| PR changes... | Visual aid |
289	|---|---|
290	| Architecture touching 3+ interacting components (the components have *directed relationships* — who calls whom, who owns what, which skill delegates to which) | **Mermaid** component or interaction diagram. Do not substitute a table — tables cannot show edges. |
291	| Multi-step workflow or data flow with non-obvious sequencing | **Mermaid** flow diagram |
292	| State machine with 3+ states and non-trivial transitions | **Mermaid** state diagram |
293	| Data model changes with 3+ related entities | **Mermaid** ERD |
294	| Before/after performance or behavioral measurements (same metric, different values) | **Markdown table** |
295	| Option or flag trade-offs (same attributes evaluated across variants) | **Markdown table** |
296	| Feature matrix / compatibility grid | **Markdown table** |
297	
298	**When in doubt, ask: "Does the information have edges (A → B) or does it have rows (attribute × variant)?"** Edges → Mermaid. Rows → table. Architecture has edges almost by definition.
299	
300	**When to skip any visual:**
301	- Sizing routes to "1-2 sentences"
302	- Prose already communicates clearly
303	- The diagram would just restate the diff visually
304	- Mechanical changes (renames, dep bumps, config, formatting)
305	
306	**Format details:**
307	- **Mermaid** (default for topology). 5-10 nodes typical, up to 15 for genuinely complex changes. Use `TB` direction. Source should be readable as fallback.
308	- **ASCII diagrams** for annotated flows needing rich in-box content. 80-column max.
309	- **Markdown tables** for parallel-variation data only.
310	- Place inline at point of relevance, not in a separate section.
311	- Prose is authoritative when it conflicts with a visual.
312	
313	Verify generated diagrams against the change before including.
314	
315	### Numbering and references
316	
317	Never prefix list items with `#` in PR descriptions — GitHub interprets `#1`, `#2` as issue references and auto-links them.
318	
319	When referencing actual GitHub issues or PRs, use `org/repo#123` or the full URL. Never use bare `#123` unless verified.
320	
321	### Applying user focus
322	
323	If the user provided a focus hint (e.g., "emphasize the benchmarks", "this needs to read as a migration not a feature"), incorporate it alongside the diff-derived narrative. Treat focus as steering, not override: do not invent content the diff does not support, and do not suppress important content the diff demands simply because focus did not mention it. When focus and diff materially disagree (e.g., focus says "include benchmarking" but the diff has no benchmarks), surface the conflict to the user rather than fabricating content.
324	
325	---
326	
327	## Step F: Compose the title
328	
329	Title format: `type: description` or `type(scope): description`.
330	
331	- **Type** is chosen by intent, not file extension or diff shape. `feat` for new functionality, `fix` for a bug fix, `refactor` for a behavior-preserving change, `docs` for doc-only, `chore` for tooling/maintenance, `perf` for performance, `test` for test-only. Where `fix` and `feat` could both seem to fit, default to `fix`: a change that remedies broken or missing behavior is `fix` even when implemented by adding code. Reserve `feat` for capabilities the user could not previously accomplish. The user may override.
332	- **Scope** (optional) is the narrowest useful label: a skill/agent name, CLI area, or shared area. Omit when no single label adds clarity.
333	- **Description** is imperative, lowercase, under 72 characters total. No trailing period.
334	- If the repo has commit-title conventions visible in recent commits, match them.
335	
336	Breaking changes use `!` (e.g., `feat!: ...`) or document in the body with a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer. Do not apply either marker without explicit user confirmation — they trigger automated major-version bumps in some release tooling.
337	
338	---
339	
340	## Step G: Compose the body
341	
342	Use the project PR-body contract first. The following order is a fallback for unconstrained sections, not permission to omit template fields or add forbidden sections:
343	
344	1. **Opening** -- the narrative frame from Step C, at the depth chosen in Step D. Under a heading (e.g., `## Summary`) if the description uses any `##` headings elsewhere; a bare paragraph otherwise.
345	2. **Body sections** -- only the sections that earn their keep for this change: what changed and why, design decisions, tables for data, visual aids when complexity warrants. Skip empty sections entirely.
346	3. **Test plan** -- only when non-obvious per the writing principles. Omit otherwise.
347	4. **New concepts section** -- only when Step B2 produced one or preserved one from the existing PR body.
348	5. **Evidence block** -- only the preserved or freshly captured block from Step B, if one exists. Do not fabricate or placeholder.
349	6. **Spec-First footer** -- for a new body use the existing plain-text default only when the project body contract permits it. On rewrite preserve existing branding without duplication; do not add or remove it merely as cleanup. Explicit user/project branding direction takes precedence.
350	7. **贡献者 trailers** -- 仅按 Step C 的已核实条件添加，放在 body 最后一个段落；无适用贡献者则省略。
351	
352	**Footer:**
353	
354	```markdown
355	---
356	
357	Built with [Spec-First](https://github.com/sunrain520/spec-first)
358	```
359	
360	The footer contains no externally loaded image and does not publish the harness or model slug. The repository link is navigated only when a reader chooses it; rendering the PR body makes no third-party image request.
361	
362	---
363	
364	## Step H: Compression pass
365	
366	Before applying, audit the body against the material claims from Step D:
367	
368	- Is the umbrella itself an outcome — what is now different for someone using this — rather than the mechanism that produced it? Check this before the two questions below: both compare against the umbrella, so both pass just as readily when it is mechanism-shaped.
369	- Does the title express Step A's umbrella outcome instead of one cluster or mechanism?
370	- Does the opening express that same umbrella, covering every peer outcome at parity? If one outcome leads while peers appear only as "also" or "comes with", rewrite from the written map.
371	- Does the map record program placement or `none`? Include known program context when relevant, and remove any invented series when none is supported.
372	
373	- Is every claim the diff cannot establish present, and is any claim the diff does show restated needlessly?
374	- Is decision-changing evidence stated as a result rather than collapsed into an unexplained "tests passed"?
375	- Are demonstrated results, assumptions, and mixed or negative outcomes clearly distinguished?
376	
377	Then apply these cuts:
378	
379	- Preserve every required template field/checklist. If an optional body section restates content already in the `## Summary`, remove it. The Summary plus the diff should carry the reader.
380	- If "Testing" or "Test plan" has more than 2 paragraphs, compress to bullets.
381	- If a "Commits" section enumerates the commit log, remove it — GitHub shows it in its own tab.
382	- If an optional "Review" or process-oriented section lists how to review, remove it. Move any truly non-obvious review hints inline with the relevant change.
383	- If the body has 5+ H3 subsections that each describe one mechanism, consolidate them into a single table row per mechanism under one header. Reserve prose H3 callouts for 2-3 genuine design decisions.
384	- If the body exceeds the sizing-table target by more than 30%, compress the longest non-Summary section by half.
385	- If any other sentence or section can be cut without lowering reviewer confidence, cut it. Do not remove project-required content or permitted preserved teaching/evidence solely to shorten the narrative. Exact-template restrictions override optional footer/teaching defaults. 保留 Step C 核实的 contributor credit 和适用 trailers，不为缩短文案删去真实来源。
386	
387	**Value-lead check.** Re-read the first sentence of the Summary. If it describes what was moved around, renamed, or added ("This PR introduces three-tier autofix..."), rewrite to lead with what's now possible or what was broken and is now fixed ("Document reviews previously produced 14+ findings requiring user judgment; this PR cuts that to 4-6.").
388	
389	Large PRs benefit from selectivity, not comprehensiveness.
390

# PR Description Writing

How to resolve the right commit range and compose a PR title and body. Loaded on demand by `spec-commit-push-pr` callers — do not load earlier.

Step Pre-A resolves the commit range, diff, and (for existing PRs) the current PR body. Steps A through H assume Pre-A's outputs are in context.

---

## Core principle

The diff is already visible on GitHub. The description exists to explain what the diff cannot show: what was impossible before and is now possible, what was broken and is now fixed, and which shape changed. Cut any sentence a reader could reconstruct from the diff itself.

- Bad (lists what was edited): "Adds `branch-creation.md`, modifies `spec-commit-push-pr/SKILL.md`, and updates contract tests."
- Good: "Default-branch shipping now verifies a fresh base before any PR work touches the branch."
- Bad (states how the work was done): "The shipping reference now anchors branch verification to a named checklist."
- Good: "Shipping to the default branch now catches a stale base before any PR work touches the branch."

If the lead sentence describes what was edited rather than what is now different for someone using this, rewrite it — this applies to every section, not just the opening, and restating the diff is the default failure mode this reference exists to prevent. A mechanism written in an outcome's grammar is judged by the same condition: "now anchors its checks to a named framework" is how the work was done, while a mechanism that *is* what the reader gets stays.

For user-facing bugs, run an extra before/after pass before writing the mechanism: name what the user would have seen before and what they now see instead. Only then mention the technical cause or fix, and only if it helps the reviewer understand risk.

---

## Project PR-body contract

Before composition, use active project instructions, then inspect standard PR-template locations relative to the confirmed repository root: root `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, `docs/`, `.github/` and `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/`. Read only applicable templates and directly referenced contribution guidance. Resolve multiple templates from the caller's change category or existing PR; ask only if a consequential template choice remains unresolved.

Required headings, fields, order, checklists and boilerplate outrank this reference's default layout. A minimum template permits useful additions; an exact/template-only contract does not. Preserve truthful unchecked/not-run fields rather than checking them by inference. Fit outcomes, validation and provenance into permitted sections; suppress optional teaching, diagrams and footer when the contract forbids them. Do not scan unrelated documentation or create a template parser.

## Step Pre-A: Resolve the PR commit range and diff

Determine which commits and diff the description should cover. Run this first; Steps A and beyond assume the commit list and full diff are in context.

### Mode

- **Current-branch mode.** Describe the captured HEAD vs the caller's resolved base, otherwise the confirmed default base. Used when the caller has no explicit PR reference (Step 6 of spec-commit-push-pr's full workflow; description-only mode without a PR ref).
- **PR mode.** Describe a specific PR's commit range. Used by the Description Update workflow (the existing PR on the current branch) and description-only mode (the user pasted a PR URL/number). The PR ref may be a bare number, `#NN`, `pr:NN`, or a full URL — the caller passes it to `gh pr view <ref>` directly. (`gh pr view` accepts numbers and URLs natively; `#NN` and `pr:NN` need the `#` or `pr:` stripped before passing.)

### Resolve PR metadata (PR mode and current-branch-with-existing-PR)

```text
gh pr view <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo> --json number,baseRefName,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefOid,headRepository,headRepositoryOwner,isCrossRepository,url,body,state
```

If the returned `state` is not `OPEN`, report `"PR <number> is <state>; cannot generate description"` and exit gracefully — do not invent a description.

### Detect the base branch and remote

For PR mode (or current-branch mode with an existing PR), use `baseRefName` from the metadata above. For current-branch mode without an existing PR, resolve in priority order:

1. **Caller-supplied base** (if the caller passed `base:<ref>`) — validate it in the confirmed base repository; do not substitute a same-named ref from a fork.
2. **Repo default branch** — `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref origin/HEAD`, strip `origin/` prefix.
3. **GitHub metadata** — `gh repo view <host/owner/repo> --json defaultBranchRef`. Parse the returned value; do not guess from common branch names.

If none resolve, keep the base unresolved and ask only for that missing fact. A local branch named main is not evidence of the intended base.

For the **base remote**, parse `owner/repo` from the PR URL (or use the repo of the current checkout in current-branch mode without a PR) and match against `git remote -v` fetch URLs (handle both `git@github.com:owner/repo` and `https://github.com/owner/repo` forms; strip `.git`). The matching remote name is `<base-remote>`. **If no remote matches** (fork-based PR with no `upstream` remote), do NOT default to `origin` — `origin` would diff against the wrong base. Skip directly to Case B.

### Case A — base remote matched, attempt local git

Bind the description to exact source identity. In PR mode use the metadata's `baseRefOid` and `headRefOid`, never a potentially stale `<remote>/<branch>` merely because it resolves. In current-branch mode capture HEAD and the resolved base commit; disclose a cached/offline base as such. Full shipping uses the separate fresh-base contract in `branch-creation.md`.

Run each command separately, replacing placeholders with validated literal values and inspecting the actual exit status:

```text
git rev-parse --verify <base-sha>^{commit}
git rev-parse --verify <head-sha>^{commit}
git merge-base <base-sha> <head-sha>
git log --oneline <merge-base>..<head-sha>
git diff <merge-base>...<head-sha>
```

Fetch only missing objects from the matched base remote. Capture and validate each result before consuming it; do not use shell variables, pipelines, redirects or command substitution to hide failures. If merge-base fails, use the API fallback for a known PR rather than inventing a range. Uncommitted changes are context only and must not be described as published PR contents.

### Case A inner fallback — SHA fetch rejected

When a PR head SHA fetch is rejected, a separate single-ref fetch may retrieve `refs/pull/<number>/head` from the confirmed base repository:

```text
git fetch --no-tags <base-remote> refs/pull/<number>/head
git rev-parse --verify FETCH_HEAD
```

Capture the returned SHA immediately and compare it with the metadata head. A mismatch requires refreshed PR metadata and a newly bound range; do not quietly compose against mixed revisions. Missing base objects still require a valid fetch or API fallback. Never parse FETCH_HEAD with shell-specific awk/substitution or assume the last of multiple fetched refs is the PR head.

### Case B — API only

Use Case B when:
- No local remote matches the PR's base repo (fork-PR, cross-repo PR), OR
- Case A's fetches all fail (offline, restricted network, expired auth, GHES quirks blocking both SHA and `refs/pull/N/head`).

Skip local git entirely:

```text
gh pr diff <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo>
gh pr view <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo> --json commits,headRefOid,baseRefOid
```

Read metadata again after API diff/commit retrieval and compare both head/base SHAs. If either changed, discard the mixed snapshot and refresh within a bounded retry; continued movement leaves composition pending. Note the API fallback and source identity in the caller handoff. Without a known PR and a valid local range, return the missing evidence instead of guessing.

### Empty range

If the resulting commit list is empty (HEAD already merged into the base, or the branch has no unique commits), report `"No commits to describe"` and exit gracefully — do not invent a description.

---

## Step A: Classify commits

Scan the commit list and classify each commit:

- **Feature commits** -- implement the PR's purpose (new functionality, intentional refactors, design changes). These drive the description.
- **Fix-up commits** -- iteration work (code review fixes, lint fixes, test fixes, rebase resolutions, style cleanups). Invisible to the reader.

When sizing the description, mentally subtract fix-up commits: a branch with 12 commits but 9 fix-ups is a 3-commit PR.

Build a compact **scope map** from the complete oneline commit list and final three-dot diff resolved in Pre-A. Use subjects for full-range coverage, then use the final diff to merge overlapping work, remove fix-up-only outcomes, and correct stale subjects. Read fuller messages only when a subject remains unclear or contradicts the diff. Group material outcomes into clusters, identify each cluster's claims, and name one umbrella outcome covering them. Never derive that umbrella from the latest commit, tracker title, branch name, original request, or opening incident alone. The story of how work started is one cluster's origin, not the whole change.

Check program placement using only context already available: the user request, a known plan, existing PR body, commit messages, or explicit series language. If this is part of a program, name the program outcome, this PR's contribution, and known preceding or follow-on work. Do not invent a series or scan all open PRs just for this check.

Before composing, write the finished map as a short run-local working note: umbrella outcome; clusters and their material claims; program placement or `none`. State the umbrella as what is now different for someone using this, never as the mechanism that produced it — the title and the opening both inherit the map's altitude, so a mechanism-shaped umbrella is not something a later step can correct. Keep it to three or four lines. This is drafting context, not another section to publish in the PR body. Step H audits the title and opening against this written map rather than memory.

---

## Step B: Decide on evidence

Decide whether to include an evidence section in the body.

**Evidence is useful** when the diff changes behavior or makes a material claim a reviewer cannot establish from the diff alone: UI, CLI output, API behavior with runnable code, generated artifacts, workflow output, ranking or scoring logic, deployment/config behavior, migrations, performance, or compatibility.

**Evidence is normally unnecessary** for:
- Inert documentation, changelog-only edits, release metadata, test-only changes, or pure internal refactors with no material reviewer claim
- Behavior requiring unavailable credentials, paid/cloud services, bot tokens, deploy-only infrastructure, or hardware not provided

Classify files by runtime purpose, not extension. Markdown or YAML may be inert prose, but it may also be runtime agent instructions, configuration, generated product content, policy code, or deployment behavior. Do not auto-skip evidence merely because a change is labeled docs-only or uses a prose-oriented extension.

**Decision logic:**

1. **Existing PR body contains a `## Demo` or `## Screenshots` section with image embeds:** preserve it verbatim unless the user's focus asks to refresh or remove it. Include the preserved block in the body.
2. **No existing evidence block:** omit the evidence section entirely unless the caller already captured evidence and passed it in.

Do not label test output as "Demo" or "Screenshots". Place any preserved evidence block before the Spec-First footer.

---

## Step B1: Related work and closing semantics

Collect known references from the request, caller handoff, current PR body, selected template and already-available commit/plan/debug context. Read a relevant fuller commit message only when its reference or intent is unclear. Do not search for plans or scan unrelated issues to manufacture provenance.

Distinguish a closing reference from a neutral relationship. Closing requires evidence that the PR fully resolves the item, known tracker syntax and the actual target conditions. For GitHub Issues, use closing keywords only when targeting the confirmed default branch and resolving the whole issue; a partial fix, investigation, validation-only change or non-default target gets a neutral link. Preserve exact cross-repository identity with a full URL or `owner/repo#number`. Unknown tracker semantics or uncertain intent never acquire closing keywords.

On rewrite, preserve existing related references and their meaning. If an existing closing line conflicts with the verified scope/target, retain the reference as neutral and explain that correction; do not silently keep a harmful close or drop its provenance. Follow project tracker conventions without imposing a universal label. Keep non-closing IDs in a separate neutral related-work line, away from close/fix/resolve phrases that integrations could interpret as actions. A PR body can trigger tracker automation; writing style does not authorize an additional tracker action.

---

## Step B2: Judge new concepts

Decide whether the change introduces a concept: a pattern, technique, library, or domain idea that a reader of this repo would plausibly not know. Skip this step entirely when the skill's concept teaching gate is off or the project's exact-template contract forbids the section.

**Gather candidates from the diff first.** Read the Pre-A diff for concept-shaped novelty: a dependency put to first real use, a technique the diff visibly introduces, or a domain idea the code now encodes. Most PRs surface no candidate; stop there and compose no section. Absence is the common case, and this path costs zero extra tool calls.

**Check each candidate against the base ref, never the working tree.** The working tree contains this PR's own code, so grepping it finds the concept you just added and wrongly concludes it is already established. Check the base instead, using the base resolved in Pre-A:

```text
git grep -il -e <term> <base-sha>
```

Run one call per candidate. Candidates cap at two, so the cost stays bounded. Inspect the exit status: 0 means matches, 1 means no matches for that term, and other failures leave coverage unknown. Read at most the needed matches; no match alone does not prove a concept is absent under other terminology.

A candidate is teachable only when it is both new to this codebase in this PR and transferable beyond it. Never teach routine use of an already-established repo pattern, ordinary refactors, renames, dependency bumps, or project-internal plumbing with no transferable idea. When in doubt, omit; a missing section costs little, while a patronizing one trains readers to skip the feature.

In the `gh` fallback path (fork PR, no local base refs), judge from diff context alone and lean conservative: compose the section only when the concept is unmistakably new.

- Bad: teaching "dependency injection" because a PR added one constructor argument in a codebase full of DI.
- Good: teaching infinite scroll on the PR that replaces pagination with it for the first time.

**Compose the section** under the heading `## New concepts` for at most 2 concepts. When more qualify, teach the most load-bearing concepts and name the rest in one sentence. Per concept, write roughly 10-25 lines covering:

1. **What it is**: the concept in plain words, no jargon dependency.
2. **Why here**: why it was chosen over the obvious alternative this PR could have used.
3. **One example from this PR**: how the shipped behavior exercises the concept.
4. **When not to use it**: one sentence on the boundary.

Format by material:

| Material | Show |
|----------|------|
| Architecture, relationships, boundaries | Fenced `mermaid` block (`flowchart TB`) |
| Code behavior, a diff's mechanics | Fenced code block with a one-line why comment above |
| A comparison or trade-off | Pipe-delimited table, prose verdict underneath |

Lead with the point, then the mechanism, then the caveat. Dense is good; long is not. Never hand-draw box-drawing or ASCII diagrams. The section is additive to Step D's sizing: a small PR that introduces a heavy concept still gets the section, and the section never counts against the base description's size rows.

**Rewrite preservation:** when rewriting an existing PR body, preserve an existing `## New concepts` section and any explainer-doc link verbatim, same as `## Demo`, unless the user's focus asks to refresh the concepts. Also preserve caller-written decision-record sections — `## Known Residuals` and `## Post-Deploy Monitoring & Validation` — verbatim: they are durable review records owned by the calling workflow (e.g., `spec-work` shipping), not description prose to regenerate; if they look stale, flag the mismatch in the handoff instead of silently dropping them. Description-only and description-update runs never write repo files.

**Archival hook:** when `spec-commit-push-pr` confirms the apply and `pr_teaching_archive` is on in full workflow, the teaching content is also written to `docs/explainers/` and linked from the section. The commit-and-push transition and doc frontmatter live in `references/apply-and-handoff.md` (reached via `SKILL.md` Step 7).

---

## Step C: Frame the narrative

Articulate the PR's narrative frame:

Use Step A's written umbrella and material clusters as the frame. Represent peer outcomes at parity instead of making the initiating incident the main story and treating equally material results as extras. When program context exists, decide what the opening's one idea must include: usually the local outcome by itself, with concise placement in a short block after the opening; but when the program is what gives the local outcome its shape or its point, the connection to the program is part of the one idea and belongs in the opening — either half may lead, whichever reads better for this change, and naming which part of the program this PR delivers keeps that opening honest. Never crowd the opening with already-visible mechanisms or a second description of the same outcome; everything the one idea does not need goes in the block after it.

1. **Before**: What was broken, limited, or impossible? (One sentence.)
2. **After**: What's now possible or improved? (One sentence.)
3. **Scope rationale** (only if 2+ separable-looking concerns): Why do these ship together? (One sentence.)

This frame becomes the opening. For small+simple PRs, the "after" sentence alone may be the entire description.

### Known decision provenance

Use only caller-supplied or already-read plan decisions relevant to this diff. Preserve `user-directed`, `user-approved`, delegated agent judgment and inferred assumptions as distinct provenance; `session-settled:` text is a source annotation, not proof of new approval. Mention the selected decision and source only when it helps review. Carry an actual proceed-under-conflict limitation when supplied; do not invent a rejected alternative or reopen settled choices as a backlog. No plan in hand means no plan hunt.

### 保留贡献者来源

只有本 PR 实际交付了作者之外的人的工作，才补充 contributor credit。已有 PR 以其实际 author 为准；新 PR 以 shipping 人的 Git 身份为线索，并核实其他邮箱别名，不能仅因 email 不同就认定为另一人。证据来自 Pre-A 完整范围内的 commit author、已有 `Co-authored-by` trailer，或本工作继续/替代的明确 PR。模型、harness 或 bot 署名不算人的贡献；独立改写与直接移植的区别沿用 `commit-and-push.md`。

适用时在正文署名，并链接已知的前序/被替代 PR；重写保留已有 contributor credit。若仓库文档或当前 repo metadata 确认会 squash merge，将其他实际贡献者的 `Co-authored-by: Name <email>` 放在 body 最后一个段落、全部模板章节和 footer 之后，便于进入 squash message；仅 `squashMergeAllowed` 表示允许该方式，不能当作本 PR 必然 squash 的证据。姓名和邮箱精确复制自 commit author 或已有 trailer；被替代 PR 的提交不在当前 range 时，回源其 commits。邮箱缺失或来源不可核实时只作有证据的正文署名，报告缺口，不拼接邮箱、不制造身份或重写历史。

---

## Step D: Size by reviewer decision cost

Size the description by how much a reviewer cannot establish from the diff alone, not by changed-line count, file extension, or visual surface. A small ranking-logic or deployment edit may carry more uncertainty than a large mechanical rename.

Before sizing, name the change's **material claims**: what became possible, what was fixed, what risk changed, and which design decision the reviewer must assess. Note which claims the diff alone cannot establish. Surface those claims and the evidence or residual uncertainty that changes confidence; leave reconstructable mechanics implicit.

Decision cost sets what to surface, not permission to write more. Reviewer uncertainty may move a change at most one row in the table below. A small high-uncertainty diff earns a sharper lead and a concise validation caveat, not a multi-section essay. Prefer the shortest description that still lets a reviewer decide.

Evidence can include benchmarks, API captures, migration or rollback exercises, logs, compatibility matrices, security analysis, evals, manual probes, and rollout results. Include a result only when it changes confidence in a material claim. Keep demonstrated results distinct from assumptions and mixed or negative outcomes.

Subtract fix-up commits when sizing. Large PRs need more selectivity, not more content.

| Change profile | Description approach |
|---|---|
| Small + simple (typo, config, dep bump) | 1-2 sentences, no headers. Under ~300 characters. |
| Small + non-trivial (bugfix, behavioral change) | Short narrative, ~3-5 sentences. No headers unless two distinct concerns. |
| Medium feature or refactor | Narrative frame (before/after/scope), then what changed and why. Call out design decisions. |
| Large or architecturally significant | Narrative frame + up to 3-5 design-decision callouts + 1-2 sentence test summary + key docs links. Target ~100 lines, cap ~150. For PRs with many mechanisms, use a Summary-level table to list them; do NOT create an H3 subsection per mechanism. Reviewers scrutinize decisions, not inventories — the diff and spec files carry the detail. If you find yourself writing 10+ subsections, consolidate to a table. |
| Performance improvement | Include before/after measurements if available. Markdown table works well. |

The table is calibration, not a diff-size formula. When in doubt, choose the shortest row that still carries the decision-relevant context, evidence, and residual uncertainty.

---

## Step E: Apply writing principles

### Writing voice

If the repo has documented style preferences in context, follow those. Otherwise:

- Preserve exact identifiers, thresholds, paths, error text and negative results when they carry the claim; plain language must not erase technical meaning.
- Active voice. No em dashes or `--` substitutes; use periods, commas, colons, or parentheses.
- Vary sentence length. Never three similar-length sentences in a row.
- Do not make a claim and immediately explain it. Trust the reader.
- Plain English. Technical jargon fine; business jargon never.
- No filler: "it's worth noting", "importantly", "essentially", "in order to", "leverage", "utilize."
- Digits for numbers ("3 files"), not words ("three files").

### Writing principles

- **Lead with value**: Open with what's now possible or fixed, not what was moved around. The subtler failure is leading with the mechanism ("Replace the hardcoded capture block with a tiered skill") instead of the outcome ("Evidence capture now works for CLI tools and libraries, not just web apps"). For user-facing bugs, lead with the visible before/after before naming the implementation mechanism.
- **No orphaned opening paragraphs**: If the description uses `##` headings anywhere, the opening must also be under a heading (e.g., `## Summary`). For short descriptions with no sections, a bare paragraph is fine.
- **Describe the net result, not the journey**: The description covers the end state, not how you got there. No iteration history, debugging steps, intermediate failures, or bugs found and fixed during development. This applies equally when regenerating for an existing PR: rewrite from the current state, not as a log of what changed since the last version. Exception: process details critical to understand a design choice.
- **When commits conflict, trust the final diff**: The commit list is supporting context, not the source of truth. If commits describe intermediate steps later revised or reverted, describe the end state from the full branch diff.
- **Explain the non-obvious**: If the diff is self-explanatory, don't narrate it. Spend space on things the diff doesn't show: why this approach, what was rejected, what the reviewer should watch.
- **Use structure when it earns its keep**: Headers, bullets, and tables aid comprehension, not mandatory template sections.
- **Markdown tables for data**: Before/after comparisons, performance numbers, or option trade-offs communicate well as tables.
- **No empty sections**: If a section doesn't apply, omit it. No "N/A" or "None."
- **Test plan — only when non-obvious**: Include when testing requires edge cases the reviewer wouldn't think of, hard-to-verify behavior, or specific setup. Omit when "run the tests" is the only useful guidance. When the branch adds test files, name them with what they cover.
- **No Commits section**: GitHub already shows the commit list in its own tab. A Commits section in the PR body duplicates that without adding context. Omit unless the commits need annotations explaining their ordering or shipping rationale.
- **No Review / process section**: Do not include a section describing how the reviewer should review (checklists of things to look at, process bullets). Process doesn't help the reviewer evaluate code. Call out specific non-obvious things to scrutinize inline with the change that warrants it.

### Visual communication

Include a visual aid only when the change is structurally complex enough that a reviewer would struggle to reconstruct the mental model from prose alone.

**The core distinction — structure vs. parallel variation:**

- Use a **Mermaid diagram** when the change has **topology** — components with directed relationships (calls, flows, dependencies, state transitions, data paths). Diagrams express "A talks to B, B talks to C, C does not talk back to A" in a way tables cannot.
- Use a **markdown table** when the change has **parallel variation of a single shape** — N things that share the same attributes but differ in their values. Tables express "option 1 costs X, option 2 costs Y, option 3 costs Z" cleanly.

Architecture changes are almost always topology (components + edges), so Mermaid is usually the right call — a table of "components that interact" loses the edges and becomes a flat list. Reserve tables for genuinely parallel data: before/after measurements, option trade-offs, flag matrices, config enumerations.

**When to include (prefer Mermaid, not a table, for architecture/flow):**

| PR changes... | Visual aid |
|---|---|
| Architecture touching 3+ interacting components (the components have *directed relationships* — who calls whom, who owns what, which skill delegates to which) | **Mermaid** component or interaction diagram. Do not substitute a table — tables cannot show edges. |
| Multi-step workflow or data flow with non-obvious sequencing | **Mermaid** flow diagram |
| State machine with 3+ states and non-trivial transitions | **Mermaid** state diagram |
| Data model changes with 3+ related entities | **Mermaid** ERD |
| Before/after performance or behavioral measurements (same metric, different values) | **Markdown table** |
| Option or flag trade-offs (same attributes evaluated across variants) | **Markdown table** |
| Feature matrix / compatibility grid | **Markdown table** |

**When in doubt, ask: "Does the information have edges (A → B) or does it have rows (attribute × variant)?"** Edges → Mermaid. Rows → table. Architecture has edges almost by definition.

**When to skip any visual:**
- Sizing routes to "1-2 sentences"
- Prose already communicates clearly
- The diagram would just restate the diff visually
- Mechanical changes (renames, dep bumps, config, formatting)

**Format details:**
- **Mermaid** (default for topology). 5-10 nodes typical, up to 15 for genuinely complex changes. Use `TB` direction. Source should be readable as fallback.
- **ASCII diagrams** for annotated flows needing rich in-box content. 80-column max.
- **Markdown tables** for parallel-variation data only.
- Place inline at point of relevance, not in a separate section.
- Prose is authoritative when it conflicts with a visual.

Verify generated diagrams against the change before including.

### Numbering and references

Never prefix list items with `#` in PR descriptions — GitHub interprets `#1`, `#2` as issue references and auto-links them.

When referencing actual GitHub issues or PRs, use `org/repo#123` or the full URL. Never use bare `#123` unless verified.

### Applying user focus

If the user provided a focus hint (e.g., "emphasize the benchmarks", "this needs to read as a migration not a feature"), incorporate it alongside the diff-derived narrative. Treat focus as steering, not override: do not invent content the diff does not support, and do not suppress important content the diff demands simply because focus did not mention it. When focus and diff materially disagree (e.g., focus says "include benchmarking" but the diff has no benchmarks), surface the conflict to the user rather than fabricating content.

---

## Step F: Compose the title

Title format: `type: description` or `type(scope): description`.

- **Type** is chosen by intent, not file extension or diff shape. `feat` for new functionality, `fix` for a bug fix, `refactor` for a behavior-preserving change, `docs` for doc-only, `chore` for tooling/maintenance, `perf` for performance, `test` for test-only. Where `fix` and `feat` could both seem to fit, default to `fix`: a change that remedies broken or missing behavior is `fix` even when implemented by adding code. Reserve `feat` for capabilities the user could not previously accomplish. The user may override.
- **Scope** (optional) is the narrowest useful label: a skill/agent name, CLI area, or shared area. Omit when no single label adds clarity.
- **Description** is imperative, lowercase, under 72 characters total. No trailing period.
- If the repo has commit-title conventions visible in recent commits, match them.

Breaking changes use `!` (e.g., `feat!: ...`) or document in the body with a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer. Do not apply either marker without explicit user confirmation — they trigger automated major-version bumps in some release tooling.

---

## Step G: Compose the body

Use the project PR-body contract first. The following order is a fallback for unconstrained sections, not permission to omit template fields or add forbidden sections:

1. **Opening** -- the narrative frame from Step C, at the depth chosen in Step D. Under a heading (e.g., `## Summary`) if the description uses any `##` headings elsewhere; a bare paragraph otherwise.
2. **Body sections** -- only the sections that earn their keep for this change: what changed and why, design decisions, tables for data, visual aids when complexity warrants. Skip empty sections entirely.
3. **Test plan** -- only when non-obvious per the writing principles. Omit otherwise.
4. **New concepts section** -- only when Step B2 produced one or preserved one from the existing PR body.
5. **Evidence block** -- only the preserved or freshly captured block from Step B, if one exists. Do not fabricate or placeholder.
6. **Spec-First footer** -- for a new body use the existing plain-text default only when the project body contract permits it. On rewrite preserve existing branding without duplication; do not add or remove it merely as cleanup. Explicit user/project branding direction takes precedence.
7. **贡献者 trailers** -- 仅按 Step C 的已核实条件添加，放在 body 最后一个段落；无适用贡献者则省略。

**Footer:**

```markdown
---

Built with [Spec-First](https://github.com/sunrain520/spec-first)
```

The footer contains no externally loaded image and does not publish the harness or model slug. The repository link is navigated only when a reader chooses it; rendering the PR body makes no third-party image request.

---

## Step H: Compression pass

Before applying, audit the body against the material claims from Step D:

- Is the umbrella itself an outcome — what is now different for someone using this — rather than the mechanism that produced it? Check this before the two questions below: both compare against the umbrella, so both pass just as readily when it is mechanism-shaped.
- Does the title express Step A's umbrella outcome instead of one cluster or mechanism?
- Does the opening express that same umbrella, covering every peer outcome at parity? If one outcome leads while peers appear only as "also" or "comes with", rewrite from the written map.
- Does the map record program placement or `none`? Include known program context when relevant, and remove any invented series when none is supported.

- Is every claim the diff cannot establish present, and is any claim the diff does show restated needlessly?
- Is decision-changing evidence stated as a result rather than collapsed into an unexplained "tests passed"?
- Are demonstrated results, assumptions, and mixed or negative outcomes clearly distinguished?

Then apply these cuts:

- Preserve every required template field/checklist. If an optional body section restates content already in the `## Summary`, remove it. The Summary plus the diff should carry the reader.
- If "Testing" or "Test plan" has more than 2 paragraphs, compress to bullets.
- If a "Commits" section enumerates the commit log, remove it — GitHub shows it in its own tab.
- If an optional "Review" or process-oriented section lists how to review, remove it. Move any truly non-obvious review hints inline with the relevant change.
- If the body has 5+ H3 subsections that each describe one mechanism, consolidate them into a single table row per mechanism under one header. Reserve prose H3 callouts for 2-3 genuine design decisions.
- If the body exceeds the sizing-table target by more than 30%, compress the longest non-Summary section by half.
- If any other sentence or section can be cut without lowering reviewer confidence, cut it. Do not remove project-required content or permitted preserved teaching/evidence solely to shorten the narrative. Exact-template restrictions override optional footer/teaching defaults. 保留 Step C 核实的 contributor credit 和适用 trailers，不为缩短文案删去真实来源。

**Value-lead check.** Re-read the first sentence of the Summary. If it describes what was moved around, renamed, or added ("This PR introduces three-tier autofix..."), rewrite to lead with what's now possible or what was broken and is now fixed ("Document reviews previously produced 14+ findings requiring user judgment; this PR cuts that to 4-6.").

Large PRs benefit from selectivity, not comprehensiveness.

13	- Bad (lists what was edited): "Adds `branch-creation.md`, modifies `spec-commit-push-pr/SKILL.md`, and updates contract tests."

15	- Bad (states how the work was done): "The shipping reference now anchors branch verification to a named checklist."
16	- Good: "Shipping to the default branch now catches a stale base before any PR work touches the branch."
17	
18	If the lead sentence describes what was edited rather than what is now different for someone using this, rewrite it — this applies to every section, not just the opening, and restating the diff is the default failure mode this reference exists to prevent. A mechanism written in an outcome's grammar is judged by the same condition: "now anchors its checks to a named framework" is how the work was done, while a mechanism that *is* what the reader gets stays.
19	
20	For user-facing bugs, run an extra before/after pass before writing the mechanism: name what the user would have seen before and what they now see instead. Only then mention the technical cause or fix, and only if it helps the reviewer understand risk.
21

23	
24	## Project PR-body contract
25	
26	Before composition, use active project instructions, then inspect standard PR-template locations relative to the confirmed repository root: root `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, `docs/`, `.github/` and `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/`. Read only applicable templates and directly referenced contribution guidance. Resolve multiple templates from the caller's change category or existing PR; ask only if a consequential template choice remains unresolved.
27	
28	Required headings, fields, order, checklists and boilerplate outrank this reference's default layout. A minimum template permits useful additions; an exact/template-only contract does not. Preserve truthful unchecked/not-run fields rather than checking them by inference. Fit outcomes, validation and provenance into permitted sections; suppress optional teaching, diagrams and footer when the contract forbids them. Do not scan unrelated documentation or create a template parser.
29	
30	## Step Pre-A: Resolve the PR commit range and diff
31	
32	Determine which commits and diff the description should cover. Run this first; Steps A and beyond assume the commit list and full diff are in context.
33	
34	### Mode
35	
36	- **Current-branch mode.** Describe the captured HEAD vs the caller's resolved base, otherwise the confirmed default base. Used when the caller has no explicit PR reference (Step 6 of spec-commit-push-pr's full workflow; description-only mode without a PR ref).
37	- **PR mode.** Describe a specific PR's commit range. Used by the Description Update workflow (the existing PR on the current branch) and description-only mode (the user pasted a PR URL/number). The PR ref may be a bare number, `#NN`, `pr:NN`, or a full URL — the caller passes it to `gh pr view <ref>` directly. (`gh pr view` accepts numbers and URLs natively; `#NN` and `pr:NN` need the `#` or `pr:` stripped before passing.)
38	
39	### Resolve PR metadata (PR mode and current-branch-with-existing-PR)
40	
41	```text
42	gh pr view <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo> --json number,baseRefName,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefOid,headRepository,headRepositoryOwner,isCrossRepository,url,body,state
43	```
44	
45	If the returned `state` is not `OPEN`, report `"PR <number> is <state>; cannot generate description"` and exit gracefully — do not invent a description.
46	
47	### Detect the base branch and remote
48	
49	For PR mode (or current-branch mode with an existing PR), use `baseRefName` from the metadata above. For current-branch mode without an existing PR, resolve in priority order:
50	
51	1. **Caller-supplied base** (if the caller passed `base:<ref>`) — validate it in the confirmed base repository; do not substitute a same-named ref from a fork.
52	2. **Repo default branch** — `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref origin/HEAD`, strip `origin/` prefix.
53	3. **GitHub metadata** — `gh repo view <host/owner/repo> --json defaultBranchRef`. Parse the returned value; do not guess from common branch names.
54	
55	If none resolve, keep the base unresolved and ask only for that missing fact. A local branch named main is not evidence of the intended base.
56	
57	For the **base remote**, parse `owner/repo` from the PR URL (or use the repo of the current checkout in current-branch mode without a PR) and match against `git remote -v` fetch URLs (handle both `git@github.com:owner/repo` and `https://github.com/owner/repo` forms; strip `.git`). The matching remote name is `<base-remote>`. **If no remote matches** (fork-based PR with no `upstream` remote), do NOT default to `origin` — `origin` would diff against the wrong base. Skip directly to Case B.
58	
59	### Case A — base remote matched, attempt local git
60	
61	Bind the description to exact source identity. In PR mode use the metadata's `baseRefOid` and `headRefOid`, never a potentially stale `<remote>/<branch>` merely because it resolves. In current-branch mode capture HEAD and the resolved base commit; disclose a cached/offline base as such. Full shipping uses the separate fresh-base contract in `branch-creation.md`.
62	
63	Run each command separately, replacing placeholders with validated literal values and inspecting the actual exit status:
64	
65	```text
66	git rev-parse --verify <base-sha>^{commit}
67	git rev-parse --verify <head-sha>^{commit}
68	git merge-base <base-sha> <head-sha>
69	git log --oneline <merge-base>..<head-sha>
70	git diff <merge-base>...<head-sha>
71	```
72	
73	Fetch only missing objects from the matched base remote. Capture and validate each result before consuming it; do not use shell variables, pipelines, redirects or command substitution to hide failures. If merge-base fails, use the API fallback for a known PR rather than inventing a range. Uncommitted changes are context only and must not be described as published PR contents.
74	
75	### Case A inner fallback — SHA fetch rejected
76	
77	When a PR head SHA fetch is rejected, a separate single-ref fetch may retrieve `refs/pull/<number>/head` from the confirmed base repository:
78	
79	```text
80	git fetch --no-tags <base-remote> refs/pull/<number>/head
81	git rev-parse --verify FETCH_HEAD
82	```
83	
84	Capture the returned SHA immediately and compare it with the metadata head. A mismatch requires refreshed PR metadata and a newly bound range; do not quietly compose against mixed revisions. Missing base objects still require a valid fetch or API fallback. Never parse FETCH_HEAD with shell-specific awk/substitution or assume the last of multiple fetched refs is the PR head.
85	
86	### Case B — API only
87	
88	Use Case B when:
89	- No local remote matches the PR's base repo (fork-PR, cross-repo PR), OR
90	- Case A's fetches all fail (offline, restricted network, expired auth, GHES quirks blocking both SHA and `refs/pull/N/head`).
91	
92	Skip local git entirely:
93	
94	```text
95	gh pr diff <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo>
96	gh pr view <ref> --repo <host/owner/repo> --json commits,headRefOid,baseRefOid
97	```
98	
99	Read metadata again after API diff/commit retrieval and compare both head/base SHAs. If either changed, discard the mixed snapshot and refresh within a bounded retry; continued movement leaves composition pending. Note the API fallback and source identity in the caller handoff. Without a known PR and a valid local range, return the missing evidence instead of guessing.
100	
101	### Empty range
102	
103	If the resulting commit list is empty (HEAD already merged into the base, or the branch has no unique commits), report `"No commits to describe"` and exit gracefully — do not invent a description.
104
